CHURCH UNION.

Annual Report of the American Congregational Union.

NEW YORK, May 12.—The American Congregational Union's annual report showed an encouraging condition of its affairs. The working capital is $55,339; direct receipts from all sources, $43,722; contributions from 961 churches, increase over previous year, $184. Grants or loans have been made to several to churches; forty-eight grants, amounting to $21,462, have been paid, and grants have been pledged to fifty-eight other churches. In addition to the cash necessary to pay pledged grants, the society holds in trust $2777 for special cases, mostly on the Pacific coast, and, deducting these amounts from the funds on hand, the society has a pledged balance of $2,000. The expenses for the year aggregate about $6000.

SPREADING THE GOSPEL.

Summary of Operations of the Bible Society for the Past Year.

NEW YORK, May 12.—The thirty-first annual meeting of the American Bible society was held at the Biblehouse this afternoon. The annual report shows: Life membership, 18; new auxiliaries organized, 39; receipts for the year, $06,484, of which $19,573 was from legacies. $266,229 in payment for books and the remainder from donations and other sources; $64,648 has been appropriated for foreign work during the year. Of the bible 1,083,696 copies were issued at the Biblehouse, 3390 imported from abroad, 275,983 printed abroad, 540,938 purchased, 1,158,498 issued at home and 316,105 abroad; of those issued to the Biblehouse, 27,749 were sent abroad; 3564 volumes were issued for the blind, making an aggregate of 12,349 volumes. In thirty-eight years, since the organization that issues the cheapest of books, 88,882,818. The gratuitous work for the year was $342,585; of this amount $108,120 was in cash appropriations to foreign lands. Besides grants of the scriptures sent from this country, 218,900 copies of the Bible Society Record have been circulated. By the employment of 198 colporteurs, 202,588 volumes of the scriptures cheapened, 188,561; desisture families supplied, 84,191; individuals in addition, 42,915, and Sabbath-school supplies, 89. Total circulation in foreign lands, 340,854 copies; 213 persons employed as distributors in foreign lands.

JEWS IN RUSSIA.

Outrageous Persecutions in Kieff-Flying Across the Austrian Frontier.

VIENNA, May 12.—A merchant of Lemberg received a telegram from Kieff to-day, stating that the whole Jewish court known as Podelh had been burned. The damage is estimated at 30,000,000 roulés. Crowds of refugee Jews are crossing the Austrian frontier at Podanlozeycka.

Scene of the Outrages.

ST. PETERSBURG, May 12.—To-day's papers are full of accounts of the anti-Jewish riots in the south and southwest. There was two day's rioting at Beresouka, in the government of Cherson. Shops were pillaged and three Jewish houses burned. There was a serious encounter between the peasants and village authorities at Vietowok, in the government of Odessa, owing to the authorities trying to recover stolen property. Troops were wounded from Odessa. At Kieff the troops are stationed in the streets. One person was killed and eighteen wounded. There have been fourteen hundred arrests. The municipal council is deliberating with closed doors on measures to prevent further disturbances. The chief ringleaders were strangers who came from the north. Near the town of Jevwinila there was Tuesday of Jewish houses and shops were destroyed. There are similar accounts from many other places. Two special trains of refugee Jews have arrived from Berdicheff. A battalion of infantry was sent from Tiraspot, Monday, to suppress the riot at Ananjeff, where all the houses of the Jews have been destroyed. Two committees have been formed at Epiphany church to assist Jews for the assistance of individual sufferers from the violence of the mob, and the other composed of Christians, to relieve families. Four hundred persons have been arrested at Balta, where proclamations have been issued inciting the Christian inhabitants against the Jews.

WENT WEST TO REFORM. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. OMAHA, Neb., May 12.—Annie Mackay, who was tried and acquitted in Chicago for the murder of Dora Abell, came to Omaha a few weeks ago with the avowed intention of reforming, and obtained employment in a hotel. On Sunday she left her place, got drunk, and went to the City Hotel to board. This afternoon she robbed the landlady's trunk of $65, and was arrested and lodged in jail to-night. A DEAD THIEF.
BALTIMORE, May 12.—Alfred Wiggins, a negro harbor-thief, was discovered in a small boat this forenoon stealing grain from the sohooner Ida, lying in the harbor. Policeman Dorsey got in a row-boat and chased Wiggins, catching up with him, when the negro knocked him down with an oar. Dorsey then shot Wiggins in the thigh, when he fell overboard and was drowned. The body was found, and the Coroner exonerated Dorsey.

JAIL DELIVERY.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

ATLANTA, Ga., May 12.—Yesterday the Pickens County jail was opened by a band of disguised moonshiners, and Ace Patterson, sentenced to the gallows for murder, released. A number of other occupants of the jail were given their liberty, but the jail-breaking was for the purpose of liberating Patterson.

FOUR YEARS AT JOLIET.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

BLOOMINGTON, Ill., May 13.—Two months ago Ed Tucker, of Springfield, while going to Chicago on the Alton Road, was condemned out of $100 by R. L. Crawford, a professional trickster. Crawford to-day was awarded four years at Joliet by the jury in the McLean Circuit Court.

A SALOON FRACAS.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

DUNQUE, In., May 12.—A fract occurred in a saloon on Sixth street this evening, in which Eugene Moorhouse was dangerously stabbed three times in the neck by one Matthew Kyne. One of the wounds was within a quarter of an inch of the jugular vein. Moorhouse's condition is critical.

HELD FOR TRIAL.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

BATTLE CREEK, Mich., May 12.—Charles Moore and Mrs. Carrie L. Hall, the adulterous couple, were brought into court to-day and waived examination. They were thereupon held to trial at the June term of the Circuit Court, and, not being able to obtain the $1,200 ball asked, were committed to jail.

WICKED NEWSPAPER MEN.
MILWAUKKE, Wis., May 12.—A special dispatch states that a brutal fight occurred at Black River Falls, Wis., between two rival editors—T. F. Hollister, editor of the Democrat, and B. J. Castle, editor of the Independent. Castle pulled out nearly all of Hollister's beard and terribly beat him.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

ATLANTA, Ga., May 19.—William Geller, a desperate character, while drunk this morning shot one woman, cut two others, and then attempted to kill himself by cutting his throat with a knife. He will probably recover, but two of the women will die.

CHARLESTON, S. C., May 13.—In Spartanburg County, Berryman W. Hicks, age 60, killed his wife, first shooting her and then cutting her throat. He immediately made two attempts at suicide by cutting his own throat. Hicks was arrested.

SHOT HIS TENANT.

CINCINNATI, O., May 12.—Michael Cain became involved in a quarrel with John Sauerbrock, his tenant, in the eastern part of the city to-night, and shot him in the face, indicting a wound that is regarded as fatal. Cain gave himself up to the police.

A DEAD BABY.
Des Moines, Ia., May 12.—Lizzie Apland, a Swede servant, gave birth yesterday to a baby, which was this morning found in a privy-vault horribly mutilated and partly eaten by rats.

GRAYSON, KY., March 29.—Bands of men styling themselves Regulators have inaugurated a reign of terror in portions of this and the adjoining County of Greenup by their unlawful depredations against the public. At Hunnewell Furnace, four miles below here, in Greenup County, on the Eastern Kentucky Railroad, a party of irresponsible ruffians attempted to control the business action of the Furnace Company. Failing in this, they restored to foul means, and the Company has been obliged to arm its employees to protect its property.

About the first of the present month Mr. Sebastian Gifort, Superintendent of the Hunnewell Furnace dispatched his son and clerk, Joseph Gifort, to Virginia to engage a force of ore-diggers. The young man returned with about forty negroes, who were at once put to work on the ore-banks. The employment of these black men incensed the so-called Regulators, and they sent notices to Mr. Gifort and his son to leave the country or suffer the penalty, death. No attention was paid to these anonymous proclamations.

On the night of the 20th inst., about twelve or fifteen of the Regulators met a party of the black-ore diggers in Browntown, near the Furnace. A brisk fight ensued and several shots were fired. One of the negroes received a face wound and a Regulator named Jones received a bullet through his groin. The blacks retreated to the Furnace and claimed protection, whereupon Superintendent Gifort armed about two hundred employees of the Furnace and prepared to give the Regulators battle. A BAD NIGGER,

Whose Neck Should Broken as Soon as He is Caught.

LITTLE ROCK, August 9.—The police have been busy since Saturday working up a case, but so far without success. On Saturday, a negro, a stranger in the city, went to a residence near the corner of Scott and Sixteenth streets and took prisoner a bright mulatto girl. He claimed to be a deputy-sheriff, and served a paper on the girl, who is only about fifteen years of age, and commanded her to go with him to the court. Knowing no better she put on her hat and started. The pretending officer took her into the woods just south of the city, drew a revolver on her, and under penalty of immediate death compelled her to accede to his hellish desires. His purpose accomplished, he left his victim more dead than alive lying in the woods. Some hours after she made her way back to the house, still at the point of death, suffering intense agony. FORT SMITH, ARK.

An Indian Convicted of Murdering a White Man.

FORT SMITH, August 9.—Sawquaree, a full-blood Sac and Fox Indian, was committed in the United States Court to-day for the murder of an unknown white man in that country in 1879. The jury were out only an hour. It appeared from the evidence that the white man had been employed by Sawquaree to make some rails for him, and while en route to the latter place was attacked by him, shot, and afterward scalped. The scalp was presented about a month later by the noble red man to his nephew, to whom he told the details of the crime. All the witnesses against him were members of his own tribe.

The annexed telegram was received here to-day:

"POWHESKA, L. T., August 9, 1881.

"To V. Dell, United States Marshal:

"I have been in pursuit of Little Buck for five days, and run on him to-day. He, with five others showed fight, resulting in the killing of Little Buck. The Indians are reported in gangs, waiting for me to pull out. I am compelled to wait a day or two for the excitement to subside.

"L. W. MARKS, Deputy Marshal."

Little Buck is one of the chiefs of the Osage tribe of Indians, which, although one of the wealthiest tribes in the Territory, is the most lawless. At the last term of court here six Osages were convicted of horse-stealing, and sentenced to imprisonment at Detroit. Deputy Marshal Marks and his posse, while on their way to this place, were besieged by a band of about 100 Indians, who demanded their release. After much parlying he was allowed to proceed, on a promise that he would not again invade the Territory. It is feared here that he will experience much difficulty in getting out of the country in safety.

The Sportsmen's Tournament.

BRIGHTON BEACH, C. L. June 23.—The third day of the tournament of the New York State Sportsmen's Association began with favorable weather and a large attendance. The first feature was the competing for the prize on the ties remaining from the amateur shooting of yesterday. The ties of five being first in order, there were thirty-eight contestants, at twenty-six yards' rise, nineteen of whom made a full score and were ordered back to thirty-one yards, where sixteen were counted out and only three were left in the contest. J. Langeake, of Long Island, won the first prize, value $100, and L. A. Cansmiller, of the Fountain Gun Club, the second prize, value $75. On ties of thirty-four there were sixteen men who stepped to the score, eight of whom went back to thirty-one yards, where the contest was decided by C. Lucklow, of Buffalo, winning the first, and C. Schowerer, of Brooklyn, the second prize. After this contest, number three for the R. V. Pearce diamond badge was called.

The Pennsylvania Editors Banquet.

LONG BRANCH, N. J., June 23.—General Grant, being indisposed, did not attend the banquet of the Pennsylvania editors to-night. George W. Childs, of the Philadelphia Ledger, brought his regrets. Covers were spread for about four hundred. President Chalfant, of the Editorial Association, greeted the editors and their guests, and was followed by Thomas V. Cooper. An address of welcome to the "Pennsylvania editors and their guests, the Tennessee editors," was given by Mr. Childs. Speech-making, interspersed with music, made up the rest of the night's entertainment. Secretaries Windom and Hunt, Postmaster-General James, Collector Merritt, and Thomas Murphy took an excursion this evening from Ocean Pier on the revenue cutter Chandler, returning at a late hour.

Two Negroes Lynched.

DANVILLE, VA., June 23.—A dispatch received here states that on Tuesday night Ester Hairston, a negro, and Lindsay, a negro boy, were taken from the jail of Stokes County, North Carolina, and hanged by lynchers. They were prisoners awaiting trial for assault upon two white girls. One of the girls, aged eight years, died last week from the effects of the injuries received, which was the exciting cause of the lynching.

LYNCHING.
How It Is Done in North Carolina—Two Ravishers Taken from a Jail by Masked Men and Left Dangling from a Tree.

Hton Point, N. C., June 22.—The details of the lynching of two negroes at Danbury, Stokes County, have just reached here. The place where this affair occurred is about fifty miles from the nearest telegraph-station. John Lindsay and Estes Hairston had been confined in jail for the past seven months for outraging the person of a white girl about 12 years old. Jonkins Lindsay was in jail on a similar charge, in which a white married woman named Gardiner was the victim. Ever since the lynching of the negro in Rockingham County last Saturday week for outraging a prominent lady of that county, Lindsay and Hairston had been very much concerned for their own safety, and several times expressed fears that they would be lynched.

During Monday night a band of 150 mounted and masked men rode into Danbury. A consultation was held, on the outskirts of the village, as to the best and quickest mode to be adopted to obtain possession of the prisoners. In accordance with an agreement, the party drew up to the jail and demanded of the jailers the surrender of Lindsay and Hairston. This was refused; the jail doors were forced open, and the crowd of masked men sprang through the doorway, forced open the doors to the cells of the two negroes, so eared them in a vehicle, and drove them rapidly out of town. As soon as a convoyont spot was found the party halted, formed into a square, and gave the prisoners a few moments in which to prepare for the sudden and horrible death that awaited them. After these preparations the two negroes were placed in a wagon, which was driven under a large oak tree. Matters were placed about the negroes' nooks; the ends of which were thrown over a branch of a tree, and the wagon then driven from under the men, and the two negroes were left hanging. Their bottles were discovered a few hours later where they were left. The names of those who participated in the lynching are not known. The punishment meted out to Lindsay and Hairston is generally approved by both the white and colored people in the community.

WRETCHES WHO SHOULD BE HUNG WHEN CAUGHT.
GREENSBORO, N. C., June 24.—The lynching of the two men a few days since in Stokes County for rape, and the lynching of another one two weeks ago, does not seem to have had the effect looked for by the lynchers. This morning as Lizzie Fluch, a little 10-year-old daughter of Mrs. Jennie Fluch, living near Hillsboro, was on her way to the spring, she was accosted by William Gauch, a negro of bad character. The second made an infamous proposal to the girl, who, frightened by the look in his eyes, attempted to run away. He caught her and committed a rape upon her person. He at once died, and the child now lies in a precarious condition. Citizens of the county are looking for him.

Intelligence has reached here also of an infamous offense of a similar nature at Martinsville yesterday evening. Charles Gilmor, a negro, actually went into the house of Mr. Prince Winchester, white he and his wife were absent. The sole occupant of the house at the time was Miss Winchester. Knowing Gilmor, she asked him what he wanted, and suspecting that he had crept into the house for the purpose of robbery, she ordered him out. The negro, glaring boldly at her, told her he had no idea of leaving yet, and then went on to tell her to keep quiet on pain of death. At once guessing his horrible design, the young woman began to scream for help. Gilmor attempted to commit his devilish design upon her person, and despite her great struggles would have accomplished his purpose had he not been frightened off by the sound of footsteps of neighbors attracted by the girl's screams. He barely had time to leap from the rear window before they entered the house. Posses of citizens have been hunting him all day. This is the third offense of this character committed by Gilmor. Once he was convicted of an attempt at rape and sentenced to nine years in the Penitentiary, but his counsel succeeded in having his sentence shortened. He was a few years after convicted of rape and sentenced to twenty years in the Penitentiary, but after serving nine years he was released.

A FIENDISH FATHER.
A Case of Inhumanity Almost Unparalleled.
NEWARK, O., January 26.—The man Cummins, who nailed a stick to his boy's tongue on Saturday, was arrested and brought to this city last evening, and placed under bonds of $500 to an pear before Justice Anderson to-morrow morning. He gave the required bond and was allowed to go home. Upon his arrival he again beat the boy most unmercifully. One of his neighbors came to Justice Anderson this morning, and asked that something be done with the wretch at once, or the neighbors would take the matter in their own hands. Some of our citizens have expressed a desire to help lynch the scoundrel. It is considered to be the most inhuman act that has ever been committed in this county, and the most intense indignation exists in regard to it. The reason that he punished the boy was that he was coasting contrary to his father's orders, and got his feet wet.

CINCINNATI. Jan. 27.—John Cummins.
A Terrible Penalty for Coasting.
CINCINNATI, Jan. 27.—John Cummins, a farmer, was on trial before a justice of the peace, at Newark, Ohio, yesterday, for cruel treatment of his seven-year-old son. The testimony showed that he split a stick, drove a tack in so that the point of the tack projected into the split, then opened the two parts and inserted the end of his boy's tongue. He then whipped the boy severely. The boy's offence was coasting. Cummins was held in $1,000 bail to answer to a higher court. In the meantime the boy has been placed in the custody of his uncle, who was appointed his guardian by the Probate Court.

A Brutal Father.
John Cummins, an inhuman brute, living near Newark, to punish his little seven year old son for disobeying him, took the lad to his stable and, according to his own statement when arrested, "split a sapling and placed it on the boy's tongue and drove a tack through it, tongue and all, to keep it in place;" he then tied the boy to the manger and gave him a severe and unmerciful beating, keeping him in the above position for several hours. This occurred on Saturday evening one week ago, and on the following Monday the boy was sent to school as usual. His teacher learned from him the particulars of the affair, and caused his father's arrest. He had a preliminary examination on Wednesday of last week, and was bound over to court in the sum of $1000. Mr. Ham. Smith, of this place, is an uncle of the boy, and on learning of the inhuman treatment he had received from his father, he went to Newark, and was appointed by the Court as guardian for his nephew, and brought the little fellow home with him. The cisizens of Newark were very much incensed over the brutality of Cummins in the treatment of his child, and lynching was freely talked of.

A deed most atrocious and inhuman has just occurred in Licking County, Ohio. John Cummins, a farmer of well to do circumstances, living near Amsterdam, for some misdeed of his seven-year-old son, took the boy to the barn and nailed his tongue fast to one end of a heavy stick of wood, and then tied the other end of the stick fast to the manger, and administered a most cruel beating to the boy, and left him in that condition for over two hours. This so aroused the teacher that he went to Newark and swore out a warrant for Cummins' arrest, and Constable Taylor served the warrant. To punish him his father took him to the barn, procured a hickory sapling, split it, put the boy's thumbs inside, nailed the sapling tight where it was split, then with it lifted the boy upon the side of the barn and nailed him, keeping him in this crucified state and unmercifully beating him all the while from 4 in the afternoon to 10 at night when the passers by, hearing the child's groans, released him.

France to Participate in the Yorktown Celebration.

PARIS, March 21.—The American Minister, General Noyes, presenting President Grevy with President Hayes's invitation to the French Government to send representatives to the Yorktown Centennial, said that the American people cherished a greatful remembrance of the participation of France in the establishment of American independence. The celebration of the common victory would lose much of its interest and luster if the sister republic were not represented. President Grevy expressed gratification and thanked the American Government for its recognition of the part which the French took in the work of American independence. France having shared in the labor would also share in the rejoicing. He dwelt on the marvelous development of the United States during the century of their independence, and concluded by declaring that France would be represented at the celebration. Minister Noyes thanked the President, and said that the representatives of France would be the guests of the United States Government. Minister Noyes will send a special invitation to Oscar de la Fayette and the members of his family to attend the centenary.

PORTLAND (Or.), March 21.—Miss Mary Ross, who died of an overdose of morphine on the 17th inst., had had an abortion performed on the 13th inst. Letters found point to George Marshall, now at Tacoma, as the seducer and provider of the medicine.

Origin of Brannan's Grant.

NEW YORK, March 21st.—The World says: Of the Mexican debt created in the struggle with Maximilian in 1865, an issue of $10,000,-000 was made at San Francisco. Of this issue the Commissioners recognize $504,000, $500,000 of which they state belongs to Samuel Brannan. Where the other $4,000 is they do not know. There is reason to believe that the $500,000 of bonds owned by Brannan have been recently exchanged by him for a grant of land in the northern part of the republic.

Fall of a Building.

ROCHESTER, March 21.—A three-story brick building 100 feet square, on Water street, owned by the Rochester Hydraulic Company, and occupied for manufacturing, fell in ruins this morning. The cause is believed to have been an explosion of the steam boiler used for heating the building. Joseph Schell, aged 20, was killed instantly on the sidewalk by the falling wall. Four or five other men were injured, but none fatally.

Rescue of a Kidnapped Child.

CINCINNATI, March 21.—This morning Mrs. Gray saw a woman carrying a child she believed was Thodore Kelly, a little boy two and a half years old, who had been missing since last Thursday, and for whom search was about to be made in the sewers. She followed the woman, saw her put the child into the side entrance of the premises on Central avenue. Mrs. Gray then called a policeman and had the child and woman taken to the police station, where the parents of the child were overjoyed to find their lost boy. The woman arrested gives the name of Kate Fitzgerald, and her residence as Newport, but gives no explanation of her possession of the child.

A series of fights between two rival factions of ruffians at Fisher's Station, Ind., resulted in the death of two men and the wounding of thirty-two.

ANDREW TEMPES, an Indian who murdered a white man at Fort Colville, Washington Territory, has been executed.

A DOUBLE TRAGEDY.
Officers in Search of an Assassin- The Wrong Man Killed-Corone:'s Inquest- Two Verdicts.
Yesterday morning early there was considerable interest aroused over the report that a colored man had been killed in a row at a dance on the previous night, and that his assailant had subsequently been shot by a policeman, and had died about eight o'clock in the morning at the police barracks, whither he had been removed. Upon investigating this reported double tragedy we learned the following particulars:

On Wednesday night a difficulty occurred at a house near Eastern Hall, in the vicinity of the yard of the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway, between two negroes, Elias Harris and John Lanier, which terminated in the latter shooting Harris, who fell to the ground, seriously wounded. Lanier then fled, and a physician was at once summoned to the relief of Harris. Dr. Bulloch responded, and upon examination pronounced the wound mortal. Immediately after the occurrence, Jackson Davis, colored, who was present at the time, proceeded to the police barracks and notified the officer on duty, at the same time stating that he could direct an officer to where he believed Lanier had taken refuge, the shooting having previously been reported by Sergeant Green.

Lieut. Howard, who was on duty, detailed Policemen John Crowley and W. F. Nungazer to accompany Davis, and the party left the barracks shortly after ten o'clock and were pillowed by their guide to the junction of the White Bluff road and the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway, about one mile and a half from the city, where are located the quarters for the station hands of the road. On reaching this point the party knocked at the door of the house occupied by Mr. F. M. Murray, the section master, and inquired if there were any strange negroes in his camp. He arose, stating that he did not know, but would accompany the officers and Davis to one of the shanties, on reaching which admittance was demanded. No attention was paid to the demand for some minutes, when the door was opened by a colored man, who looked out, and perceiving the officers, immediately closed the door again and attempted to spring from the window. Finding his escape cut off from this quarter, he swung open the door, and springing outside broke into a run. Davis immediately called out "that's the man," and the officers yelled to the fugitive to stop, but he continued running, when he was fired upon several times. He fell but quickly arose and started to run again, when another shot was fired and he tumbled over on the ground. The party then approached the prostrate man, when it was discovered that he was not John Lanier but a colored man named Isaac Hicks, not the one they were after.

Hicks was found to be badly wounded, having been shot in three places, and was placed in a wagon and conveyed to the police barracks, where he received attention from Dr. J. T. McFarland, who at once pronounced him fatally wounded. He died yesterday morning early. The Coroner was no offied, and, empaneling a jury, proceeded to the barracks, where the body was viewed, and afterwards adjourned to the court house, where an inquest was opened and testimony was taken:

Lieutenant J. T. DIED OF HIS WOUND.
Death at the Infirmary of Ellias Harris. Colored-Coroner's Inquest and Two Verdicts.
Mention has been made in the MORNING News of the shooting of Elias Harris, colored, on Wednesday night by John Lanier, colored, who escaped, and whose pursuit resulted in the killing of an innocent man, Isaac Hicks. Yesterday Harris, who was conveved to the Georgia Infirmary, died from the effects of his wound, which was inflicted in the windpipe. The details of the killing are briefly these:

On Wednesday night, 27th instant, John Lanier entered the house of his husband Martin and asked for some oil, and was told by Martin he had none. He then walked across the room and stood up by the fire. Martin was engaged in writing in an account book and paid no further attention to him. Presently Aleck Martin entered the room from the back door, and was followed by Elias Harris, who went to the fire to get a light for his pipe. A few minutes after the report of a pistol was heard and Harris fell to the ground. Lanier said, "Let me get out of here," and started to run out of the door, and in doing so jumped over the body of Harris. Martin grabbed Lanier and said, "You cannot go out of here," and his brother Aleck also caught hold of him. Lanier struggled to get away, and presented his pistol in the face of Aleck Martin, when Hiram called to him not to shoot. Lanier then managed to free himself and escaped. Hiram Martin stated that the shooting was done without any provocation whatever. He did not see Lanier fire the shot, but he saw a pistol sticking in his pocket when he came into the house.

There were in the house at the time Hiram Martin and his wife, Aleck Martin, Charley Cheeseborough, Anthony Crieg and Ellen Johnson, but none of them saw the sh t fired. There had been, to the knowledge of these parties, no previous difficulty between Harris and Lanier, and there was no quarrel on the night of the shooting.

The Coroner was notified and held an inquest, at which some five or six witnesses, the occupants of the house, were examined, but their testimony was in substance as above detailed. None of them had seen Lanier shoot. They only know that he had a pistol, and after the shooting jumped across Harris' body and escaped from the house.

After considering this testimony for some time, the jury failed to agree, and a majority and minority verdict was returned as follows:

We the jury do say, from the evidence before us, that the said Elias Harris came to his death from pistol shot wounds, and that the said John Lanier is guilty of the crime of murder.

LABOR RIOT IN NEW ORLEANS.
A Colored Man Shot by a Policeman and the Governor Called Upon for Troops.

NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 10.—The labor war culminated in bloodshed this morning, when James Hawkins (colored), a member of the Cotton Teamsters' Association, was shot and instantly killed by Police Sergeant Reynolds. The cause which led to the shooting was the attempted arrest of Hawkins, when a general flight ensued, during which Reynolds's clothing was torn off and missiles were thrown at his head by colored women. As the prisoner was about to escape Reynolds fired two shots. One struck Hawkins in the thigh, passed through, and hit a white man named Pat Connelly in the leg. The second shot struck Hawkins in the forehead, and he fell dead. Intense excitement was created, and matters assumed a serious aspect. Fire alarm bells were rung, which summoned the police force. Several arrests were made for interfering with teamsters. A float of cotton which had been left by the drivers was set on fire. The Mayor has ordered the Chief of Police to close all places where liquor is sold in the vicinity of the troubles, and to arrest any parties failing to comply with the order. The Mayor has forwarded the following communication to the Executive:

NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 10, 1881.

To his Excellency Louis A. Wilts, Governor of Louisiana.

SIR: The police force which I have under my control has been overpowered. I have serious apprehensions of further troubles, and do not feel that the police force alone can preserve the peace of the city. I therefore respectfully call upon your Excellency for assistance, that the preservation of the peace may be secured.

Your obedient servant, Jos. A. Snakspzare, Mayor.

The Governor issued orders to Major-Gen. Bahan to have militia regiments ordered to their armories. They were disbanded, however, early in the afternoon, there being no immediate need of their interference. It is understood, however, that they will be ready at a moment's notice.

There was no more trouble after the killing of Hawkins, with the exception that some teamsters returning from the Commercial Press were stoned and hooted at the corner of Orange and Chippawa streets, at 4 P. M. When Officer Brehter ordered the mob to stop he was hit with a stone, and he fired twice without effect.

TRAIN WRECKERS.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LA CROSSE, Wis., Sept. 10.—A cowardly attempt was made late last night to wreck a freight train on the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad at a place called Scheider's Crossing, about a mile and a half from this city. The villains had piled a large quantity of wood and boards on the track, but had done it so clumsily that the engine scattered the rubbish on either side of the track and only a few pieces remained or got under the engine, and they did no material damage. This is the third attempt that has been made to wreck trains at this crossing, and no clue has been found to the guilty parties.

A FEELING OF INDIGNATION.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

HOT SPRINGS, Ark., Sept. 10.—An ineffectual attempt to secure and lynch a negro charged with attempting to outrage Mrs. J. Parker, an elderly lady, yesterday, was made last night. A body of armed men surrounded the jail and endeavored to break in, but were met by a steady fire from the jail guards and about a hundred negroes ambushed a short distance away. There is a feeling of intense indignation that the negroes should attempt to defend the most heinous of crimes. Trouble is anticipated.

CAPITAL AND LABOR.

Collision Between the Striking Laborers and Police in New Orleans—A Negro Killed—Trouble Feared Monday.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

NEW ORLEANS, La., Sept. 10.—The difficulty which evil-disposed persons have for the past ten days tried to bring about culminated in the killing by a policeman of a negro striker who refused to submit to arrest. This caused great excitement, and negro men and women thronged the levee and adjacent streets. Capt. Minor, Chief of the Labor Bureau of the cotton factors, was shot and stoned by negro women. Considerable of a panic followed, and the general alarm was sounded calling out the full police force. The negroes were massed in one quarter of the town, and, having no leadership, nothing was done with them. At noon the Mayor, under influence of some panic, called on the Governor for troops, alleging the police were overpowered. The Governor ordered Maj.-Gen. Behan to respond to the Mayor's request with such full force as was necessary, but on consultation discovered that the militia mainly sympathized with the strikers, and they were not called out. Mean-time the excited crowd dispersed, no other trouble being reported than the occasional brickbating of a non-unionist teamster by irresponsible men and boys. It was thought during the day that an adjustment was being reached, but the action of the authorities during the day seems to have embittered the strikers, and negotiations were declared off. A massmeeting of all the strikers was held tonight, when it was determined to give the dead negro a heroic burial—white and black cooperating. More trouble is threatened on Monday.

MEMPHIS, Tenn., Sept. 10.—An agent from New Orleans is here trying to get men from the compresses to go to New Orleans to take the places of the strikers, offering as high as $10 a day. The papers here advise the men not to go, and it will have effect. All here employed are doing well, getting good wages, and are not willing to risk it at New Orleans. Very few, if any, and it is the belief generally that none, will go.

A Negro Killed—The Savannah Contingent Alarmed—Funeral of the Victim—The Cotton Exchange and the Various Unions.
NEW ORLEANS, September 10.—The levee was almost clear of cotton yesterday morning. Eight cotton presses had steam up and were engaged in compressing. The Laborers' Executive Council have placed the entire case in the hands of the Arbitration Committee of the Chamber of Commerce. The Employers' Association refuse to leave their side of the question to outside arbitration, being determined, if possible, to compel the labor representatives to make a settlement direct with the employers.

This morning as wagons were leaving the Coopers' Cotton Press the strikers interfered with the teamsters. A police Sergeant ordered the strikers to disperse, when he was knocked down and beaten. He drew his revolver and shot one of the strikers, a negro, through the head, killing him instantly. Two white men were wounded. The Mayor has called out the entire police force. Capt. F. O. Minor, while driving along in a cab, was shot at twelve times, but escaped unhurt.

The Governor, in response to a communication from Mayor Shakespear, issued an order to Major General Behan to have the militia regiments ordered to their armories. They were disbanded, however, early in the afternoon, there being no immediate need of their interference. It is understood, however, they will be ready at a moment's notice. There was no more trouble after the killing of Hawkins, with the exception that some teamsters returning from the Commercial Press were stoned and hooted at the corner of Orange and Chippewa streets at 4 p. m. When officer Brechster ordered the mob to stop, he was hit with a stone and he fired two shots. Nobody was hurt.

At four o'clock fire was discovered in the after hatch of the steamer Cella. The hatches were closed and nine burning bales of cotton taken out.

Negotiations looking to a compromise are in progress. The factors demand prerogatives of employing labor and full control of the cotton trade; also the rescinding from the by laws of the Cotton Men's Association of everything relative to labor, leaving the association only a benevolent organization. There are rumors that everything will be settled by Monday.

NEW ORLEANS, September 11.—The killing of Hawkins by Sergeant Reynolds yesterday, which seems to have had no other justification than his intimidation of colored laborers, produced a bad effect on the colored men who came here recently from Savannah, Ga., some of whom called at the City Hall to procure means to be sent back home, but failed to meet the Mayor.

The report that the welghers had seceded from the union has been confirmed in part, but a number of them still maintain their organization and do not intend to yield. The stevedores have entered into an arrangement with the ship agents and brokers. The screw men refuse to sever their connection with the labor union.

The longshoremen last night decided to "hold the fort" and to attend Hawkins's funeral this morning. It is stated that two prominent stevedores have declined to put their men to work to-morrow in up-town ships unless they are provided with a militia guard.

The Employers' Association is anxious to have the screwmen withdraw from the Laborers' Union. It could then ignore the longshoremen, yardmen and teamsters. PITTSBURG, September 12.—A destructive fire broke out about 12 o'clock this morning in Siemans & Anderson Steel Works, in the upper part of the city. THE COTTON STRIKE.
The strike of the New Orleans cotton laborers assumed a very serious aspect on Saturday and Monday last. Strikers congregated on the streets in crowds and assaulted the drivers of cotton floats with stones and clubs, and several serious affrays grew out of the attempts of the police to quell these disturbances. Fortunately only one life was sacrificed—that of a colored man named James Hawkins, who was shot and instantly killed by Sergeant Reynolds of the police while resisting arrest. Finding his means for preserving the peace and protecting the commerce of the city inadequate, Mayor Shakespeare called upon Acting Governor McEnery for aid and the militia was ordered to assemble. Although the occasion seemed to justify the active employment of the State troops to maintain the supremacy of law and order, they were kept cooped up in their armories and rendered no service whatever. Mayor Shakespeare has sharply criticised the inaction of Gen. Behan in the premises and we are inclined to regard his strictures pertinent and deserved. Tuesday night after a long conference of committees representing the Employers Association and the several labor organizations, a basis of compromise was agreed upon which brought the strike to an end. Some modifications in the tariff of charges for handling cotton were made, and the employers carried the point for which they have so strenuously contended from the first, viz: the right to employ and discharge hands free from the interference or dictation of labor unions.

CEDAR RAPIDS, Ia., June 8.—The Coroner's jury, after a thorough investigation as to the cause of the railroad disaster Sabbath morning last on the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad, four miles west of this city, whereby Frank Horton and Thomas Hurley were killed, returned a verdict this afternoon, finding that the death of these two men was caused by the "culpable and criminal negligence of Charles B. Crop reports from Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Texas and Arkansas indicate that in Ohio and Indiana the wheat outlook is good except in Southern Indiana. In Kentucky the wheat prospect is poor. In Ohio the peaches are in some places partially and in others totally killed. In Kentucky the fruit prospect is good. In Arkansas and Texas the late peaches are killed. The early corn was hurt by the heavy rains and the acreage of cotton is reduced.

Mr. Gladstone yesterday gave notice that the government will on Monday ask leave to introduce a bill amending the Parliamentary oath.

A crowd of five thousand persons assembled at New Pallas yesterday, where an attempt was being made to evict some tenants. Five hundred military and police were present, but the Sheriff was stoned. The police charged several times upon the crowd, but the bailiff's life being threatened the evictions were for the time foregone.

William McIntosh killed his sister in New York yesterday because she refused to give him money.

The New York stock market yesterday was marked by many fluctuations, but it became strong at the close at an advance. The sales were 278,105 shares.

Marshall Baxter was hanged at Charlotte yesterday for the murder of Bob Hennegen, in January last.

The Czar is reported to favor repressive measures without example in Russian history.

Sir Charles Dilke stated yesterday in the House of Commons that the Fortune Bay negotiations were still proceeding.

The Texas Western Railway has been incorporated with a capital of $30,000,000.

Sparks from a passing locomotive caused a fire in Fort Worth, Texas, by which $70,000 worth of cotton was destroyed.

John Gothard, colored, was hanged at Towsontown, Md., yesterday for the murder of Joseph Woods.

John Wend, charged with murder, was shot by a mob in Paris, Kentucky, Thursday morning.

At Allendale, S. C., on Thursday William Prieste was probably fatally wounded by his son, who fired at him five times.

Mrs. Christian Koch and her three children were found with their throats cut in St. Paul yesterday. The mother is credited with the butchery.

An outbreak of the White River Utes is feared.

Four persons were drowned on Wednesday by the upsetting of a sail boat on Lake St. Claire.

Serious anti-Jewish riots are reported to have occurred at Argeenan, West Prussia, and in the Russian Province of Kherson.

What is supposed to be a volcano has been discovered in Ohio county, Kentucky. A lot of corn shock were set on fire by the burning gas emanating from the ground.

The efforts to unite the Arkansas Democrats on the Fishback amendment question have failed.
The damage by the Missouri freshet is put at over four million dollars.

Geo. Maronia was fatally shot by Antonio Mucisto at Buffalo, N. Y., on the 1st inst. It is alleged that the man Maronia insulted Mucisto's wife.

At Galveston, Texas, on the 30th ult., Sam Brown cut his wife's throat and then his own. A little nine-year-old child attempted to take the razor and was badly cut. Brown was insane.

A few days since three white men and one Chinese were murdered while asleep in their cabin near Sitting Springs, Inyo county, Cal. The murderers are supposed to be Chinese or Indians.

Wm. McIntosh shot his sister, Mrs. Lousia Hardy, at New York, on the 29th ult., because she refused to give him money. McIntosh, who formerly ran a liquor store, says his sister owes him over $11,000.

William Stewart, a farmer living near Dundee, Ill., was murdered and his body thrown into the Fox river, on the 29th ult. Robbery was the motive.

The body of F. Y. Folsom, a wealthy livery stable keeper of Baltimore, was picked up in the river on the 29th ult., with feet tied and hands badly bruised. It is thought he was robbed and then thrown into the river.

A mob entered the jail at Paris, Ky., on the 28th and attempted to secure a murderer named Winn in order to lynch him, Winn, when ordered from his cell, refused to obey and made preparations for defense, whereupon several shots were fired at him, with fatal effect.

A fight ensued at Covington, Ga., on the night of the 27th, between Dick Allen, Henry Hunton and three men named Allen, Young and Campbell. It seems that Hunton acted on the defensive, the others having attacked him. Allen and Young were badly cut in the back and Campbell's throat was cut from ear to ear. Hunton surrendered, but was released after a
D. McCartney, Jr., a druggist was fatally stabbed in front of his store at Pittsburg, Pa., on the night of the 27th, by Charles Dalgleish. The murderer was one of a party of loungers, whom McCartney had ordered away from his place.

T. M. Pearce, a tinner, got into a difficulty at Midway, Ky., on the 26th inst., and was shot dead by Jacob Williams, a farm hand. Pearce leaves a wife and four children.

J. W. Robb, prosecuting attorney at Astoria, Oregon, was shot dead by G. Robson, a former client.

The sheriff of Trinity county, Cal., killed a stage robber on the 27th.

Three robbers went into the house of John Baker, near Mannington, West Va., on the night of the 26th, and after failing to shoot him through a window, entered and assaulted the old man with an axe. He was felled like an ox, whereupon the villiams secured $300 and made their escape. Mr. Baker's son-in-law was up stairs at the time, but was too cowardly to go down.

A well-known character in Cincinnati, named George W. Stevens, stabbed his father-in-law, Harvey Newell, four times, inflicting fatal wounds.

Bridgeton, Mo., a point twenty miles from St. Louis, was the scene of a fearful affray on the 25th. A fight ensued infront of a saloon between Valentine Walker and James Williams, when Walker, who is a half breed, beat Williams' brains out with a stone. A farmer named Michael Revoir attempted to stay the terrible proceedings, when the enraged Walker felled him with a fence rail, inflicting probably fatal injuries.

A farmer named Legden, who was working a farm near Clifden, Ireland, from which tenants had been evicted, was shot dead by nine men who surrounded his his house on the night of the 24th. His son was severely wounded.
Two darkies at Culterville, Ill., quarreled about a woman while returning from church on the 24th inst., one of them was stabbed and killed.
A bootblack named Jesse Terrell was fatally shot in a billiard hall in Paris, Ill., by William Bowen.

A Grist from South Carolina. Special Dirvatch to The Chicago Tribune.
Columbia, S. C., Oct. 28.—Yesterday morning Horace Williams and Mack Riles, two reputable farmers living in Darlington County, went to town to sell their cotton. During the day, having drank too much liquor, they became involved in a controversy about a division of the money. A friend interfered and parted them before they came to blows, but later in the day they came together again and started for home, apparently in good spirits. On the way they stopped at a country store to replenish their whisky-flasks. Shortly afterwards they again quarreled and came to blows. Riles was getting worsted, when he drew a dagger and plunged it into the breast of his adversary, inflicting a mortal wound. Williams died in ten minutes, and the murderer was arrested.

Today Milton Owens and Wash Young, two colored men, in Newberry County, fought, and the latter was killed by a blow from the other.

Near the same place the day before Charles Jackson shot and killed Green Owens, both colored men. Both were desperate.

This morning a white woman named Mary Lewis, living in Lexington County, in this State, married a coal-black negro named Manning Law, and the couple started for Augusta, Ga., in a buggy. The brothers of the woman, who is very well connected, started out in search of the pair. At a point called Buck Creek, the two frate brothers overtook the couple. The negro, apprehending death at the hands of his pursuers, drew a pistol and began firing at them. The fire was returned, and one of the shots took effect in Law's breast, inflicting a wound which will probably prove mortal. The Lewis brothers then went to the house of the preacher who had performed the marriage ceremony and threatened to kill him. The minister ran on into the woods, and the Lewis brothers gave hot pursuit, firing as they ran. Last night late the preacher reached Columbia and gave your correspondent the above facts. He eluded his pursuers by hiding in a dense thicket, then came here by the night train. It is not known whether the negro died, or what became of his wife and her infurlated brothers.

There seems to be a persistent effort in certain quarters to hold Chicago up to the country as an ungrateful city because her contributions in aid of the farmers who suffered last August by fire in Michigan have not equated the demands or the expectations of some of the persons engaged in making collections for that purpose, although she has already refunded more to Michigan to relieve her burnt-out farmers than she received from all that State ten years ago when ten to twenty times as many of her people were in sore distress. It has pleased these people to remind Chicago that when this city was swept by fire there was no hesitation anywhere in the contribution to the relief of her stricken multitudes.

There evidently is a mistake somewhere on this subject. When Chicago was swept by fire on the eve of winter in 1871 the number of people rendered desolate and homeless was a huge one, and the benovidence of mankind was extended to them, and for this Chicago has always been grateful. The net losses in Chicago were immense—$160,000,000. The contributions of the world, however, were never disparaged because in the aggregate they did not equal 3 per cent of the losses.

The destruction of property in the Saginaw farm districts was a grievous loss to the farmers of three counties. Some hundreds of them were left destitute of even food and clothing, without homes or habitations, losing their season's crop of 1881, and thus deprived of obtaining more except by loans on their land or by charity until the next harvest. They lost all they had except the land, which was swept of its entire vegetation. The number of victims is variously estimated at 1,100 to 3,000 families, and they were all in purely agricultural districts.

These sufferers were almost all farmers, cultivating their farms. In the State of Michigan there were 125,000 other freehold farmers, all of them well to do, and able promptly to assist their suffering brethren in the Saginaw district. In the adjoining States of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, and Wisconsin, there are between one and two millions of prosperous farmers owning rich productive lands, and every one of them naturally and personally interested in the sufferings of the few hundreds of Michigan farmers who with their families had been so suddenly overtaken by this fire calamity. Now, what are the facts? The money raised in Michigan for these suffering farmers has been collected mainly in Detroit and in the other cities and towns of the State. The 125,000 prosperous farmers have practically done nothing to relieve and succor those unfortunate farmers of the Saginaw district. In Ohio, Indiana, New York, Massachusetts, Illinois, and Wisconsin, and all other parts of the country, the contributions in aid of these Michigan farmers have been made in the cities and towns, and scarcely a dollar has been forwarded or given by the agricultural brethren of the West or elsewhere to the sufferers. As a whole, the farmers of these Western States are the most wealthy and prosperous, as they are the most numerous, of the population, and yet they have left the Governor of Michigan and the other gentlemen who have been soliciting donations to importune the cities and towns of the country for aid. Notwithstanding the sufferers were almost exclusively farmers, the farmers of Michigan and all other surrounding States have done substantially nothing in the way of making good the losses of the suffering agricultural class.

The population of Chicago at the time of the fire was, and at this time is, largely made up of laborers and other workmen dependent upon their daily wages. A majority of them do not own the houses in which they live. They are, as compared with the farmers of the Western States, poor in this world's goods. The entire Chicago population lost by the fire; the rich and prosperous were left penniless, and their recovery from these losses has been exceptional. These destroyed capitalists have been succeeded by newcomers, who have brought capital here. Thousands of families once in good circumstances, who lost their entire property in the fire, still suffer under the poverty then entailed, and it is a mistake to suppose, as many of these official people in Michigan assume, that the losses of the Chicago fire were made good by the world's contributions. Four and a half millions of donations went but a small way towards making good 160 millions of loss over and above insurance recovered. But that charity saved tens of thousands of laboring poor from perishing of cold and hunger. It kept them alive until they could find work and become self-supporting.

The latest news from Great Britain shows that under the operation of the Land bill the Irish outlook is more encouraging, and the tenants are eagerly rushing forward to the Land Court to have their rents fixed by it. On Thursday last 1,500 cases were entered, and there were 30,000 applications for notices that they would apply to the court. In the County Mayo, which was a very hotbed of the league's agitation, a thousand tenants in Castlebar alone have applied to the court to fix their rents. As a matter of course, if the court fixes rentals that are moderate and satisfactory to the tenants they will withdraw from the Land League, having secured their object in joining it. Everything depends on what the Land Court does, how it applies the law, and satisfies the wishes and expectations of the farmers, who want one-third to one-half, knocked off the rents that have been tortured out of them under distress warrants and evictions. A letter from Mr. John Forsythe, printed in our last issue, throws some light upon the eagerness of the tenants in the North of Ireland to get court leases, and upon their satisfaction with the new condition of things. Mr. Forsythe refers to the sale of a farm of nineteen acres recently made in the County Autrum, in the North of Ireland, in the neighborhood he came from, which is by no means one of the best of Irish agricultural districts.

The tenant-rights in the little farm of nineteen acres, which had been paying a yearly rental of $160, or two pounds an acre ($10), was put up to auction under the provisions of Gladstone's recent Land act which Parnell despires, and was sold for $3,500, or $194.40 per acre, which represents the tenant's good-will, improvements, and interest in the farm. As Mr. Forsythe says: "Prior to the passage of the Land act the tenant could not have sold his tenant-right or good-will except by the permission of the landlord; and then only to such purchaser and at such price per acre as the landlord might determine, which in no case would exceed the sum of £10 ($50) per acre, but was generally limited to £5 ($25) per acre, depending greatly on the liberality of the landlord." Under the Gladstone Land bill the tenant is entitled to the improvements he has made, such as the buildings he has erected, the draining and manuring, and the working material he has accumulated, and not only this, but to the improvements made by former tenants, so that when he sells out his interest in the lease he obtains an equivalent for his improvements; or, should he choose to make a new lease, he still has the actual cash benefit of these improvements, as the new valuation must be made upon the naked land itself, after the value of the improvements has been deducted. In other words, the tenants for the first time in their lives are joint owners with the landlords, and in reality are owning from one-fourth to one-half of the whole value of the farms in Ireland. Coroner Matson yesterday afternoon paid a visit to Park Ridge, a suburban station on the Northwestern Road, just this side of Deplainces, for the purpose of holding an inquest upon the bodies of John and Mary Niemann, an old couple who had been struck and instantaneously killed by lightning Thursday afternoon, while driving home from Chicago along the Eliston road, only a short distance from living Park. The inquest was held at the late residence of the deceased at Park Ridge, a plain and unpretending farm-house about a mile distant from the station. Here were gathered a large concourse of people, upon whose minds the sudden taking-off of their aged friends had evidently produced a very profound impression.

As soon as the place was reached, the party were shown into the barn, where the deceased still lay at rest in the wagon in which they had met their death. The evidences of its terrible nature were evident, especially in the case of the old lady, whose body was found to be terribly scarred by the electric fluid and by the flames of her burning clothing, the lightning having set fire to the upper part of her dress. The body was clad very neatly, a black woolen shawl being thrown around a light-colored stuff dress. THE WORK OF A JURY CHOSEN FOR A PURPOSE.
A Verdict that Receives Not the Slightest Popular Sympathy or Approval - How it was Arrived at.
The trial being over and the prisoner acquitted, it is now in order to give the details and the popular opinions of this remarkable case. Neal was first tried at the May term, 1880, after a motion by Mr. Higgins, his counsel, to quash the jury panels by reason of the exclusion therefrom of men of African descent by reason of their race or color, and to remove the case to the United States District Court had been refused. He was then tried by a jury composed of the following gentlemen:

Thos. S. Dixon, Brandywine Hd.
John W. Worrell, Mill Creek.
John Williams, St. Georges.
Hyland P. Bullen, White C. Creek.
Jesse Reeves, New Castle.
Wm. Lawton, Wilmington.
James Vanarsdalen, New Castle.
Aaron H. Paxson, Pencader.
John Thompson, Mill Creek.
Richard Booth, Wilmington.
Deweese Chandler, Christiana.
Joseph H. King, Brandywine.

This jury after an hour's deliberation returned a verdict of guilty on the afternoon of May 26th, 1880, and the following day Nesl was sentenced to be hanged.

The subsequent proceedings, which resulted in a reversal of this judgment and Neal's arraignment for a second trial are well known.

On Friday last Neal's second trial was commenced, and in the drawing of the jury Mr. Higgins was careful to challenge every Democrat and every man on the jury who lived south of the canal. With the exception of the foreman, the entire jury was drawn from Christiana, Brandywine and Wilmington Hundreds, eight of them being from this city. The regular panel was exhausted, and Sheriff Clark summoned talesmen from a previously prepared list, among his names being some men who, if they lived a thousand years in Wilmington, would never be deemed worthy of having their names placed in the box to be drawn upon the regular panel. His proceedings in drawing talesmen for the Harrigan jury were in marked contrast, as on this occasion he called upon reputable and well-known citizens of New Castle county. Finally this remarkable jury, evidently chosen for a deliberate purpose, was selected, as follows:

DAVID R. CHOATE, White Clay Creek Hd.
WM. B. ADAMS, Wilmington.
NEHEMIAH DAVIS, New Castle.
WM. MURPHY, Wilmington.

SAMUEL G, LOGAN, Wilmington.
CHARLES H. HOWARD, Wilmington.
GEO. D. WATSON, Wilmington.
ALBERT I. DERRICKSON, Brandywine.
It was a representative jury in one respect, at least. It represented Republican sentiment generally and the Republican party of New Castle county most admirably.
The jury drawn the trial proceeded. The State made a plain case. The evidence of the prosecuting witness was not impeached in the slightest particular, and the defense made practically no defense whatever. Mr. Higgins gave the jury the key note in his closing argument, when he brutally said he would treat the evidence of the prosecuting witness,—the poor, outraged white woman—as a lie, for such he believed it to be. Judge Houston, in his charge, combatted this by saying that it was highly improbable a woman would make such a charge against an entire stranger, without just cause. The jury, however, took the cue. and branded the poor woman as a wretched perjurer, for the sake of the black villain whose guilt was clear as the noonday sun.

At seven o'clock Saturday evening the jury retired for consultation, and remained out all night. Sunday morning there were rumors,—which were evidently sent out from the jury room for the purpose of deceiving the public—that the jury stood ten for conviction and two for acquittal, and that finally one of the latter came over to the majority, leaving but one dissenters. The sequel shows that these reports were false, and that only two of the jury had conscience enough to maintain the guilt of the accused. Four men voted for acquittal on the first ballot while two votes for conviction and the other six by blank votes expressed their doubts in the case. One by one these six came over but the two who held out for conviction, remained true to their consciences until the eighteenth ballot, on Monday evening, when one went over to the side of acquittal, where the six doubtful (?) ones had already ranged themselves. Tuesday morning the long champion of female virtue stood at his post manfully, but after dinner he joined the ranks of the negro worshipers and the farcical verdict was formed.

It was just three o'clock when the came into court, and, with stolid expressionless faces took their seats in the jury-box. There was a brief delay while waiting for the prisoner to be brought in, and then in answer to the usual in terrogatories of the clerk, the forma pronounced the startling words, "NO GUILTY!" A silence like untodeath followed. No one moved, no one spoke. The spectators seemed as though spellbound with horror and surprise. Instinctively th

eyes of all within range sought the faces of the prisoner and his counsel. The negro sat in the box, with a simple smile upon his face, as though scarcely realizing the full extent of his wonderful good fortune. Mr. Higgins sat in the bar, with folded arms and grim visage, his features working with uncontrolled but well concealed emotions. But whatever were his feelings none shared them with him. Not a hand was extended in kindly congratulation, or a word uttered in commendation of his wonderful victory. Among all the people there assembled, he was alone in the hour of his triumph. It was a dearly bought victory.

Later in the afternoon, for fear his legally established innocence would not be accepted by the public, he was placed in a close carriage and driven to the State line, above Clay mont, where he was left to follow his own sweet will in the congenial atmosphere of Delaware county, Pa.

As to public opinion in regard to the verdict, it is sufficient to say that it is condemned by ninety nine out of every one hundred people, regardless of party feelings. The jury is execrated on every hand.

FOURTH EDITION.
THE NEAL JURY.
The Verdict of "NOT GUILTY" a General Surprise—Some Talk of Lynching the Released Man.
In a late edition of yesterday's REPUBLICAN, the verdict of the jury in the Neal case was briefly announced. To-day we are enabled to give the following particulars.

Just before the opening of Court yesterday afternoon, a bailiff came down from the jury room, and informed the Judges, who were still in their parlor, that the Neal jury had agreed upon a verdict.

The Court directed that Mr. Higgins be sentior, and that Neal be brought into the dock. After Neal was seated he remained perfectly quiet, his general expression being that of anxiety.

It was some minutes before Mr. Higgins arrived, and while waiting for him the jury were brought in.

The Clerk of the Court, polled the jury and then asked the usual question, "Do you find the prisoner at the bar guilty or not guilty, in manner and form, as he stands indicted?" A breathless silence seemed to settle over the Court room for a moment, which was broken by the voice of the foreman of the jury as he answered in a low tone "NOT GUILTY." Men who had been present during the whole trial, and listened to the chain of evidence that the State had forged around the prisoner could not believe their own ears; and asking the nearest bystander if they had heard aright, turned away thinking that an eminent Pennsylvania Judge was correct, when he said that, "no one but the Almighty knew what the verdict of a pettit jury would be."

Immediately after rendering their verdict the jury left the court room and Neal was commanded to stand up.

The Chief Justice then said: "William Neal, the jury which has tried you have rendered a verdict of not guilty and we now discharge you from custody."

Neal was taken out of the Court room between the two tipstves and conducted to a carriage which was in some mysterious manner already provided and in waiting and rapidly driven away as there were serious threats of lynching him, not only by persons outside but also by many who were in the Court room.

A number of the jurors were approached yesterday afternoon after the rendering of the verdict, but very little information could be obtained. Late last night, however, a representative of the REPUBLICAN succeeded in obtaining the following, which is believed to be correct:

Immediately after retiring on Saturday evening a ballot was taken which resulted in two for conviction, four for acquittal, and six who had not made up their minds.

Four ballots were taken on Saturday night with about the same result, and about half past ten, word was sent down to the Judges who were still in their parlor, that there was no hope of agreeing that night.

On Sunday morning several of the jurymen complained of being sick and Dr. Kirchner was called in to prescribe for them.

During Sunday a number of ballots were taken, and on the eighth and ninth, it was evident that a feeling in the prisoner’s favor was extending, as the last taken showed that there were seven men who were in favor of clearing him, only two for conviction, and three who had no settled opinion upon the matter.

On Monday nine ballots were taken making eighteen in all that had been cast. The last ballot taken on Monday night showed that there was but one man in doubt, while eleven were in favor of acquittal.

There was but three ballots taken yesterday, one in the morning, and one about noon, they both showed the same result as the last ballot cast on Monday night, eleven for acquittal and one in doubt. About half past two yesterday afternoon the twenty-first and last ballot was taken, and resulted in a verdict of acquittal.

Our informant stated that there were several considerations that influenced the jury in their actions, one of which was that they thought the evidence of Mrs. Gosser contradictory in some material points, and it was hinted that if the jury had been instructed that they could have rendered a verdict of assault, or assault with intent to commit a rape, the result might have been different.

The NEAL VERDICT.—It is a novel mode of defense which the Republican adopts in discussing the false and scandalous verdict rendered by the jury that declared Neal not guilty. That paper resorts to every possible means to rake up excuses for this act of these men, while it declares in plain and emphatic language that it does not agree with the verdict. It says:

"There is no doubt of the fact that the public mind is averse to the verdict, the evidence against Neal being of the most positive character and uncontradicted by the defense. The only doubt in the case was in regard to the resistance, whether it was sufficient, or what might be expected in a case of that kind. Coupled with that was the fact that for many years past only negroes had been executed for criminal offences while white persons equally guilty invariably were cleared."

There is the language of the Republican. It is copied verbatim from its columns. We have not abused the jury nor the Counsel for Neal. The GAZETTE has simply characterized the verdict as scandalous; as of a character that will lead men to believe the men who rendered the verdict did so in violation of the sacred oaths they had taken to render a "true verdict according to the evidence." Could their verdict be true according to the evidence? We leave the Republican to answer, and we quote its own declarations as the best answer. It is printed in italics above, but we will quote it here again. It says the "evidence against Neal being of the most POSITIVE CHARACTER and uncontricted by the defense." And this is assigned as a reason for "the fact that the public mind is averse to the verdict." We should think it was. The public mind has some respect for the wives and daughters of the men of Delaware. Why the decent negroes of the South would not render such a verdict as that. They have more respect for their own wives and daughters than to send forth such a verdict to excuse one of the worst characters that could curse a community with its presence, for committing a crime which all good men detest. Even the savage negro in the wilds of Africa would hesitate but a short while about dispatching a man who had entered his abode and violated the purity of his rude home as Neal did. That he did this the Republican says the proof is of the most positive character and uncontradicted by the defense. What laurels can counsel gain from such a verdict? A verdict rendered upon such a showing could never be worn as an adornment to the cap of a high minded member of the bar—it would never be placed as a rose upon the breast of a just and honest counsellor who held woman in the estimate that she deservedly claims in Delaware. LETTER FROM THE MOUNTAINS.
The Pleasure of Summering in the Mountain of the Schuylkill County.
Special Correspondent of the Republican.

TAMAQUA, Pa., July 5th.—Just when or by whom sea side bathing was first introduced, remains a mystery, but we know that to hie away to the mountains was in vogue, away back in the primitive days of the world's history. We read about it in the first books of the Old Testament and it is after all the best way to spend the hot summer months. In the first place it is less costly, and it is less trouble than the sea side watering places. At most of the first class hotels in this region one can obtain substantial board for ten or twelve dollars per week and we do not have to rely on stale vegetables bought in Philadelphia, and carried in the cars away down to the sea shore as they do at Cape May and Atlantic City. Here one may have pure milk and cream, fresh laid eggs, good wholesome butter, and all kinds of vegetables fresh from the gardens. We are enjoying splendid weather just now, just warm enough during the day and the night cool enough to sleep well, while such things as mosquitos are unknown. No one could wish for a better appetite than a bracing walk over the mountain side will give hem if taken in the early morning. The scenery is delightful and it is grand to see old "Sol" rising out of his misty bed beautifully tinting every little cloud and tree.

It is surprising how each succeeding event helps us to forget those that have preceded it. This is brought very forcibly to ones mind, in looking back four or five years, then the "Mollie Maguires," had full sway. No one felt safe and although your correspondent did not live hereabouts then, their whole history is reinvested with interest by hearing the people talk about them, and to read the book that Allan Pinkerton wrote, from notes taken by his detective Jas. McParlan who spent several years with the "Mollies" and became one of their most trusted friends, makes one think truly, "truth is stranger than fiction." Your correspondent visited several places where murders took place. He stood on the spot where in 1876 John P. Jones was murdered by Kerrigan, Doyle and Kelly, as he was going to his daily work. He saw the lamp post where B. F. Yost was climbing up to put out the light when in a minute he was shot dead by McGeehan, a "Mollie." He saw the rum holes where the "Mollies" used to meet which by the way are still run by the widows of some that were hung, and where McParlan, alias Jas. McKenna, used to lay around drunk to all appearances, but awake and sober, as they afterwards found out. But the days of the "Mollies" are over, they will never organize again, because they won't trust one another. McParlan was a dose they will never forget.

The P. & R. R. R. Co. are putting a very handsome fence around the open lot adjoining the depot. The 4th passed without any accidents. There was a mock circus parade, which for originality and fun making "took the rag off the bush" of anything your correspondent ever saw.

The attempted assassination of the President created intense feeling here. In Mahaney city, near here, a man named Refowitch came near near being lynched for making some disloyal remark. They had the rope around his neck when he begged so hard that they let him off.

Souirr, Que., Sept. 12.—A most disbolical murder was perpetrated last Saturday night at St. Bonaventura, a parish about twenty-seven miles from here, in the District of Ilichellen. It appears that three horse-traders, named respectively Israel Proulx, Joseph Beland, and Antolino Cote, started for St. Hyacinth the Saturday morning, where they spent the day and drank rather freely. A short time before leaving one of them was heard to say that he would soon have his revenge about some difficulty which arose amongst them. On their return to St. Bonaventura, true to his word, either Proulx or Beland struck Cote with a bottle and inflicted such injuries as to leave his victim unconscious on the roadway, where he was found the next morning. The man lingered for three hours, when death put an end to his sufferings. The Coroner, High Constable, and deputy left for the scene of the murder last evening.

SHOT BY HIS SON-IN-LAW.

Louisville, Ky., Sept. 12. Toulght about 6 o'clock, when James Montgomery came to the house of his son-in-law, Sam Duff, to leave Duff's daughter of 8 years, whom Montgomery had given a drive, the two men engaged in an altercation over old family troubles, which had resulted in a separation and divorce between Montgomery and his wife, who now lives with Duff, which resulted in Duff drawing a revolver and shooting at Montgomery five times, four of the balls taking effect. The doctors certified the wounds are not reasonably mortal, and in about three hours Duff, who had been failed, was released on ball. Montgomery is a retired tailor, an Irishman, and a funeral Orangeman. Mrs. Montgomery and Duff's family are street Romanists, and this is said to be the basis of all their trouble.

THE TRAIN-ROBBERS.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., Sept. 12.—George Banister was arrested today for disturbing public worship at a church in the vicinity of the recent Blue Cut train-robbery. While the minister was preaching he jumped up and hurrahed for the train-robbers and began firing off his pistol. He escaped at the time, but was arrested today, and from his action it is believed he has given himself away and will probably be held as one of the participants in the robbery. SHOT BY A LUNATIC.

was shot by a religious crank named Bennett, who he attempted to arrest for robbery. Since then Bennett has been at large, armed with a double-barreled shotgun, and kept the whole section at bay, $500 being offered for his capture, dead or alive. A FATAL ALTERCATION.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
Little Rock, Ark., Sept. 12—A tragic affair is reported today from Woodruff County. William Mason, a farmer living near Cotton Plant, while returning home got into an altercation with three men who were working on the road. It appears the latter ordered him to turn aside, and, when he refused, overturned his wagon. Mason then drew a revolver and killed two of the men and badly wounded the other.

STRUCK WITH A BILLIARD-CUE.

Muncie, Ind., Sept. 12.—At Yorktown, four miles west of this city, William Coppersmith and William Paedy met in a saloon and a quarrel began.
