Mixed School Row in New Jersey. A SCHOOL HOUSE BURNED DOWN BY INCENDIARIES.
An Associated Press dispatch from Fair Haven, N. J., says: Some time ago trouble arose between a white and colored resident of this place because the colored people insisted that their children had a right to attend the new school built for the white children. The colored school was finally closed, and some of the colored scholars were admitted to the white school. The white children took offence and remained from school, and upon the principal of the school demonstrating with the trustees a teacher was procured to teach the colored school. The colored people still insisted that their children had a right to receive tuition in the white school, and admonished them not to obey their colored teacher. Several threats have been made on the part of the colored people that the colored school house would be burned down. At a late hour on Wednesday night the school house was discovered to be on fire. The fire was extinguished by the white people, but a few minutes later the roof was found to be on fire. All efforts to save the building were fruitless, and it burned to the ground. The crime is attributed to the colored people, and the police are in search of Henry Johnson, a negro of bad reputation, who was seen leaving the burning building. Two fires had been started, one on the lower floor and another in the upper loft. A colored man named Henry Curtis gave valuable information against the supposed incendiaries. The excitement over the affair is intense.

RED BANK, March 15.—The school war in Fair Haven, waged between the white and colored residents, and which grew fiercer a few weeks ago, after the burning of the colored school house, assumed a new phase to-night. A meeting of white and colored citizens was held in the white school house to vote on the question of raising $1,500 to build a school house for the colored children. The school room was crowded, about fifty colored men being present. The Rev. J. K. Freed was chosen Chairman. In reply to the question of the Chairman, "What is the wish of the meeting?" the answer of Jos. Richardson, a colored man, at once showed the feeling of the colored people.

"What do we want?" cried Mr. Richardson.

"Why, every white man here knows what we want. We want a school house, and $1,500 is too small a sum to build a suitable one. We want a school house for our children as good as the white children have, or a suitable addition to the white school, so that our children may attend it."

This called forth an angry debate. Mr. Little suggested that if $2,400 built a school house that seated 200 white children, $1,500 ought to build one that would seat sixty colored children.

John Eustice moved that a school house be built for the colored children. Before the motion could be put a colored man jumped up and moved as an amendment that an addition, to cost $1,500, be built to the present white school house for the use of colored children. When this amendment was put to vote the excitement was intense, the white men giving a thundering "No, no." while the colored men with one voice voted "Yea."

The amendment was lost and the original motion was then put. The majority of the whites voted yes. When the noes were called for all the colored men were silent, the negatives given being only by whites.

After the motion had been declared carried the white men who had voted in the negative explained that they voted that way because they were not in favor of building a school house which would stand as a monument to their own stupidity. The blacks had been offered a good school and had refused it because they could not associate with the whites.

A colored man then moved that both the colored children and the white children be sent to the white school. This made the meeting wild with excitement. Half the white men were on their feet shouting, gesticulating, and calling to the Chairman. The Chairman finally decided that the motion was out of order, and that the matter must be decided by the trustees.

It was then decided to select a committee of three, consisting of two white men and one colored man, who should choose a site for a school house for the colored children, and get an estimate of the cost. The first man chosen was Jas. H. Minton. A call was then made for the colored man who was to serve on the committee. The negroes refused to name one of their own race, and all who were asked by the whites to serve refused to do so. The meeting finally selected two more white men, Wm. R. Cross and Chas. H. Hendrickson, to make up the committee.

A negro then asked what the colored children were to do while the committee was picking out a lot for their school and building the school house. The District Clerk replied that there was but one thing for them to do, namely, to stay out of the white school. The meeting was then adjourned for two weeks, when the committee will make its report.

FAIR HAVEN, N. J., March 22.—The colored people charge that the action of the School Board in closing the white school yesterday was because the colored people, at a meeting on Sunday, had determined to take action under the law passed by the Legislature last Thursday, imposing a penalty for refusing admission to a child, no matter of what color, creed or nationality, and that on Monday they would have demanded that their children be admitted to the vacant seats in the white school, and if refused would have sought redress. FAIR HAVEN, N. J., March 80.

Another episode in the war between the whites and blacks of Fair Haven came at last night. On Tuesday night nearly every voter in the district was at the school room, as well as many from Red Bank and adjoining towns. James H. Minnton, District Clerk, asked that the meeting be adjourned until Tuesday night, that Dr. Lockwood, the County Superintendent of Schools, might b present. The meeting was promptly adjourned. The men did not leave the school room, however. Joseph Richardson, the leader of the negroes, accused Minnton of putting up a job on the negroes in the school room last night was Gen. Clinton B. Fisk. He has always tried to make the negro the social equal of the whites in this neighborhood, and on several occasions he has roused a feeling of animosity in the whites by his officiousness in favor of the negro. His language last night was very temperate, and had he tried to rouse a spirit of opposition in the negroes he would have been ejected from the building. The law recently passed in the New Jersey Legislature was framed expressly for the Fair Haven case. It is said that the law was written by Robt. Allen, Jr., who had influence enough to have it passed. It provides both fine and imprisonment for any person who refuses to allow children to attend any school on account of their nationality or color.

Fish Fries.

Our people seem to have become very fond of fish of late, or of piscatorial sport. Last Wednesday we followed a small party up on Boeuf river to a place back of Mrs. Edwards' plantation, arriving there just before they began collecting the fish together for the "fry." The catch was small, but the ladies fried them very nicely, we had good coffee, and, with other things to help out, we managed to make a good meal, which we enjoy as much as any we ever ate. We all relished our dinner; all were cheerful and disposed to participate in a little good natured humor at each other's expense, and all came home well pleased with our day's sport and recreation.

Thursday we joined some of the same party, with an addition of a few others, and went up on Dead Lake, near Lafourche Ferry, where we caught an abundance of fish—more than we could all eat, though we did our best to get away with our full share. It was a very pleasant affair—as pleasant as that of the previous day; but on our return home our horse got very sick, and we thought for a while we would have to walk home and lose a horse too, but we managed to get home, after some delay.

On Friday morning, as we write this, another party are on their way to Cypress bayou to have a fish fry—hope they too will have a good time.

Some dissatisfaction exists in Grant parish at the fact that several teachers hold positions on the Parish School Board.

A negro man and a mule were struck by lightning on the plantation of Mrs. Moreland, in Tensas arish, last Saturday.

Last Saturday on the road about two miles from Minden, Webb Gamble shot and killed Frank Elkins. The shot took effect in the abdomen, and the wounded man died next day. The shooting was done about dusk. Elkins and Gamble were brothers-in-law.

The election in the parish of St. Martin for the removal of the parish seat from St. Martinsville to Breaux Bridge, held on the sixteenth instant, resulted in a grand victory for St. Martinsville, where the court-house has been located for nearly a half century.

A most atrocious crime was committed Saturday night at Kingstown, a small hamlet in DeSoto parish, about twelve miles northeast of Mansfield. M. Judd Scott, a young merchant doing business in Kingstown left his boarding house about 9 o'clock p. m., going to his store, where it was his custom to sleep. On Sunday morning his body was discovered lying about half way between Mrs 'Beard's, where he boarded, and his store. The top of his head had been almost entirely blown off by a gun shot. CRIME.
Ike Stockton, a desperado from New Mexico, was fatally shot at Durango, Col., while resisting arrest.

George W. Hunt, paying teller of the Importers' bank of New York, is charged with the embezzlement of $16,900.

W. F. BRANCH, disbursing agent of the American Transfer company at Bradford, Pa., has been arrested in Toronto for the embezzlement of $150,000.

BURKE & MEYER, wholesale cloth dealers at New York, have caused the arrest of their bookkeeper for the embezzlement of $3,000.

BILL RYAN, the Glendale train robber, was convicted at Independence, Mo., after deliberation for twenty minutes by the jury, and sentenced to imprisonment for twenty years. A motion for a new trial was instantly entered, on the ground of intimidation by Governor Crittenden's presence with armed guards.

The perpetrators of the Arkansas train-robbery have been lodged in jail at Hope, and have been fully identified. One was captured near Sulphur Bluff, Tex., and the other two in the Indian nation. Clark Hull, a conductor on the Iron Mountain road, had the satisfaction of taking one of the robbers.

A PERPERATE attempt was made, at Pallas Green, Ireland, to blow up with dynamite the residence of Captain Thomas Lloyd, occupied by seventeen emergency men and police. Captain Boycott was in Westport recently, and was followed by a mob and burned in effigy. Moffat, the leader of an Orange expedition in County Louth, was fired at and wounded.

MASON, one of the four Central Pacific train-wreckers now undergoing examination at Auburn, Cal., has made a full confession and disclosed the hiding place of tools and arms.

OTTO FREESE, of Aurora, Ill., was murdered on Main street, at midnight, Saturday, by Thomas Oleson, a Swede, 17 years of age. The affair grew out of badinage between two squads. The jail was surrounded by a large and excited crowd all the foremoon, and the prisoner was sent to the county jail at Geneva to avert a lynching.

JOHN AND FRANK McDONALD, of Memononee, Mich., having served two years in the penitentiary, returned for vengeance. They killed William Kittson and fatally stabbed his brother Norman. On the following evening a mob of four hundred battered down the jail door with heavy timber, dragged the prisoners to death on the road, and strung their bodies to trees.

For the purpose of ousting some of the directors a meeting of stockholders of the Nevada and Oregon railroad was called at Reno, Nevada. Treasurer Coffin and two gentlemen from San Francisco were ordered to retire from the room, but did not do so. In a second the air was filled with whistling bullets, fatal wounds being inflicted upon D. W. Balch, of San Francisco, and S. C. Scovill, secretary of the company.

TED FRANKS, the jailer at Bloomington, Ill., was shot through the heart on the 4th inst., by a horse thief named Chas. Pierce. Other prisoners seized the murderer and took the revolver from him. Within ninety minutes a crowd of five thousand persons surrounded the jail, the iron doors were soon forced, and Pierce was dragged out to a locust tree at the corner of Market and Centre streets, and strung up. The shrieks of the villain could be heard above the cheers of the crowd. It was expected that Patsy Devine, the assassin of Aaron Goodfellow, who occupied the cell next to Pierce, would meet the same fate, but he was spared. His being granted a new trial by the supreme court was the inciting cause of the lynching.

Murder at Aurora, Ill.

AURORA, Ill., Oct. 2.—This city has been the scene of another unprovoked murder. Shortly before midnight last night three young Swedes named Thomas Oleson, Ole Oleson, brothers, and Louis Wester, who had been drinking and playing pool in various saloons down town during the evening, started up Main street, near the Congregational church. The Olesons, Wester being on the other side of the street, met a party of young gentlemen who were on their way home from a serenading tour. The latter party had stopped to talk with a couple of friends, whom they had just met, and were singing and making merry among themselves when the Olesons came along. Some good-natured remarks were passed between the Sweedes and the other party about the singing, and Otto Freese, one of the serenaders, laid his hand in a friendly way on the shoulder of Thomas Oleson, when the latter suddenly drew a knife and stabbed Freese in the throat, severing the branches of several arteries, and inflicting a wound from which the young man bled to death before he could be removed from the place where he was struck. The murderer and his brother, as soon as the fatal blow had been given, ran off up Main street, but in a short time Ole returned to the scene of the murder, and he and Wester, who had in the meantime come up, were there arrested. He is only about 15 years old and professes not to know anything in regard to the murder. The Oleson brothers and Wester have been employed at the tile works just east of the city. Freese, has made all day it that he and his brother obtained the liquor that intoxicated them on the night of the murder from the saloon kept by Daniel Freese, the father of the murdered boy. As both the Olsons are minors, the city authorities can prosecute a suit for unlawfully selling to minors. Active raids have already been commenced against the saloonkeepers for illegal practices, prompted by the recent horrors. Four have been indicted by the grand jury. A strong sight will be made on the trial of Thomas Olson. He has a con-

SHOT DEAD.
LITTLE Rock, Ark., Oct. 10.—Intelligence reached this city today of a terrible tragedy last Saturday at a sawmill near Grand Lake, Ark., a small town on the Mississippi River. William Brooks, proprietor of the sawmill, was beating on employe when a fellow workman named Willian Yountz interfered. Brooks, exasperated, turned upon Yountz, when the latter drew a revolver and fired, the ball striking Brooks in the head and killing him instantly. Yountz was arrested, and after a preliminary examination was discharged.

A DETECTIVE'S FATE.

St. Louis, Mo., Oct. 16.—The body of an unknown man was found yesterday hanging to a tree in thick woods four miles from Grain Valley Station, on the Chicago & Alton Railroad, some twenty miles from Kansas City. The body had apparently been hanging three days. The theory is that the man was a detective, and had been lynched by some one connected with the recent train robbery.

MURDERED FOR HIS MONEY.
Evansville, Ind., Oct. 16.—A colored man named Green was found dead in the suburbs of Henderson this morning, with his head split open with a cooper's adze. A man was arrested on suspicion and lodged in jail. The adze, covered with blood and hair, was found two squares from the body. It is supposed he was murdered for his money.

NOT GUILTY.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

EAST SAGINAW, Mich., Oct. 15.—The jury in the case of Shin Robinson, John Hughes, and James and John Wilson, charged with murder in the Chesonitry circus riot, brought in a verdict of "not guilty" today. There have been two convicted, five acquitted, and two parties yet to be tried in this case.

REWARD PAID.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., Oct. 15.—The Iron Mountain Railroad Company yesterday paid Clark Hall and the four men who assisted him in capturing the train-robbers $1,000 each. Moore and Huddlestone have not yet been paid. It is rumored they will sue the company.

ARREST OF COUNTERFEITERS.
EVANSVILLE, Ind., Oct. 16.—Two men giving the names of John Miller and E. C. Brobson were arrested a mile above the city today on a charge of counterfeiting. Spurious coin, molds, metals, etc., were found on them.

Pink eye is disappearing from Jacksonville.

All Central Illinois is howling about the mud.

A Horrible Usurpation of the Law.
ATLANTA, GA, April 7.—The store of Dan Potts, in Coffee county, was robbed and burned. Willie Johns was charged with the crime and turned over to five men who took him away. Five days after the prisoner was found dead at Indian Ford, Seventeen Mile Creek. His head was shot to pieces, and a large part of his brain was clutched in one of his hands. At the coroner's inquest two of the men who went off with him swore that they did not know who killed him. It is said the guard were pitched upon by a party of armed and unknown men, who hurried Johns to Indian Ford and riddled him with bullets.

ATLANTA, April 7.—Some time ago
the store of Daniel Potts, in Coffee
County, was robbed and then burned
Suspicion pointed to a young man nam-
od Willie Johns. He was accused of
the crime, and then seized and placed in
the custody of five men.

What became of Johns afterward be-
came a mystery until to-day. A party
of hunters found his body at Indian Ford
on Seventeen Mile Creek. His head
was shot to pieces, and one of his hands
held in a death grip a large quantity of
his brains.

Upon news of the discovery, two of
the five men who took Johns away
were arrested and taken before the Cor-
oner. They both swore they knew
nothing whatever about the young man's
fate. They said that after they had
started off with him they were met by an
armed body of men on the road, who
overpowered them, took the prisoner
